               THIS INFORMATION MEMORANDUM   IS DATED 02 OCTOBER 2026             
                                                                                  
         THIS DOCUMENT IS IMPORTANT AND REQUIRES YOUR ATTENTION. YOU ARE ADVISED TO CAREFULLY
                                                                                  
         READ AND UNDERSTAND ITS CONTENTS.                                        
                                                                                  
         THIS INFORMATION MEMORANDUM IS ISSUED IN COMPLIANCE WITH THE COMPANIES ACT (CAP 486 OF
         THE LAWS OF KENYA) (THE “COMPANIES ACT”), THE CAPITAL MARKETS ACT (CAP 485A OF THE LAWS
         OF KENYA) (THE “CM ACT”) AND THE CAPITAL MARKETS (PUBLIC OFFERS, LISTINGS AND DISCLOSURES)
         REGULATIONS, 2023 (THE “REGULATIONS”).                                   
                                                                                  
         THIS DOCUMENT DESCRIBES THE SPECIFIC TERMS OF AN OFFER FOR SALE OF 2,000,000,000 ORDINARY
         SHARES OF A NOMINAL VALUE OF KES 0.20 EACH BY SOKONI RETAIL KENYA LIMITED (“SOKONI” OR
         THE “SELLING SHAREHOLDER”) (THE “OFFER SHARES”) IN THE ORDINARY SHARE CAPITAL OF QUICK
         MART PLC (THE “COMPANY” OR THE “ISSUER” OR “QUICKMART”) (THE “OFFER”). THE OFFER SHARES
         WILL RANK PARI PASSU IN ALL RESPECTS WITH THE EXISTING ORDINARY SHARES OF THE COMPANY.
                                                                                  
         THE CAPITAL MARKETS AUTHORITY (“CMA”) HAS APPROVED THE OFFER AND THE INFORMATION
         MEMORANDUM AND THE NAIROBI SECURITIES EXCHANGE (THE “NSE”) HAS APPROVED THE LISTING
         OF THE OFFER SHARES AND THEIR ADMISSION TO TRADING ON THE MAIN INVESTMENT MARKET
         SEGMENT OF THE NSE. AS A MATTER OF POLICY, THE CMA AND THE NSE ASSUME NO RESPONSIBILITY
         FOR THE CORRECTNESS OF ANY STATEMENTS OR OPINIONS MADE OR REPORTS CONTAINED IN THIS
         INFORMATION MEMORANDUM. APPROVAL OF THE ISSUE OR LISTING IS NOT TO BE TAKEN AS AN
         INDICATION OF THE MERITS OF THE ISSUER OR OF THE SECURITIES.             
                                                                                  
         IF YOU ARE IN DOUBT ABOUT THIS INFORMATION MEMORANDUM, THE OFFER OR ANY INFORMATION
         CONTAINED IN THIS INFORMATION MEMORANDUM, PLEASE CONSULT YOUR STOCKBROKER,
         INVESTMENT ADVISER, BANKER, FINANCIAL CONSULTANT, LEGAL ADVISER OR OTHER PROFESSIONAL
         ADVISER, WHO SPECIALISES IN ADVISING ON THE ACQUISITION OF SHARES AND OTHER SECURITIES.
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
         INVESTMENTS IN EQUITY OR EQUITY-RELATED SECURITIES INVOLVE A DEGREE OF RISK. FOR
         INFORMATION CONCERNING CERTAIN RISK FACTORS WHICH SHOULD BE CONSIDERED BY PROSPECTIVE
         INVESTORS, PLEASE REFER TO THE SECTION ON “RISK FACTORS AND MITIGANTS” IN THIS INFORMATION
         MEMORANDUM.

      This Information Memorandum contains information about Quick Mart PLC (“Quickmart” or “the Company” or
      the “Issuer”) in connection with the Offer, for the purpose of giving information in respect thereof, to prospective
      investors. This Information Memorandum and the Offer have been approved by the CMA. The NSE has approved
                                                                                  
      the listing and admission of the Offer Shares being offered by way of this Information Memorandum on the Main
      Investment Market Segment of the NSE.                                       
                                                                                  
      The Offer Shares rank pari-passu in all respects with all other existing Ordinary Shares in the share capital of the
      Company, including the right to receive dividends or other distributions declared, made or paid by the Company
      after the allotment of the Offer Shares.

      SBG Securities Limited (as Lead Transaction Advisor, Sponsoring Broker, and Lead Placing Agent), Stanbic Bank

      Co-Placing Agent), Coulson Harney LLP (trading as Bowmans in Kenya) (as Legal Advisor), Ernst & Young LLP (as
      Reporting Accountants), Image Registrars Limited (as Data Processing Agent and Share Registrar), Creide Limited
      (as Public Relations Advisor) and Adili Corporate Services Kenya LLP (as Corporate Governance Advisor) (all together
      the “Advisors”), have consented in writing to act in the stated capacities and to their names being included in
      this Information Memorandum and have not withdrawn their consent prior to the publication of this Information
      Memorandum.

      shares in Quickmart which would be material to that person or has a material, direct or indirect economic interest
      in Quickmart.

      Risk Warnings relating to the Information Memorandum                        
      Prospective investors are expressly advised that an investment in any Offer Shares that may be purchased pursuant
      to the Offer has certain risks and that they should therefore carefully review the entire contents of this Information
      Memorandum. Prospective investors should ensure that they read the whole of this Information Memorandum and
      not just rely on key information or information summarised within the document. Prospective investors should in
                                                                                  
      particular see the section entitled “Risk Factors and Mitigants” in this Information Memorandum when considering
      an investment in the Offer Shares.                                          
                                                                                  
      Prospective investors should consult their own professional advisers before making any investment decision with
      regard to any Offer Shares, to, among other things, consider such investment decision in light of such investor’s
      personal circumstances and in order to determine whether or not such prospective investor is eligible to purchase
      the Offer Shares. In making an investment decision, prospective investors must rely on their own examination,
      analysis and enquiry of the Issuer and any Offer Shares that may be purchased pursuant to the Offer, including the
      merits and risks involved.

        LETTER   FROM   THE  CHAIRPERSON                                          
        OF  QUICK   MART   PLC                                                    
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      Dear Prospective Investor                                                   
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      On behalf of the Board of Directors (the “Board”) of Quick Mart PLC ("Quickmart" or the "Company"), I am pleased to
      provide you with the following information in connection with our proposed initial public offering of 2,000,000,000
      Ordinary Shares of a par value of KES 0.20 each by way of an Offer for Sale (the “Offer”).
                                                                                  
      This Offer marks a defining milestone in Quickmart's evolution and reflects the Board's conviction in the Company's
      long-term prospects, strategic direction and ability to create sustainable value for all stakeholders. It also provides
      investors with an opportunity to participate in the continued growth of one of Kenya's leading modern grocery
      retailers.                                                                  
                                                                                  
      Quickmart’s journey has been characterised by resilience, adaptability and an unwavering commitment to serving
      Kenyan consumers. From its early beginnings, the Company has grown into a nationally recognised retail brand
      with a broad store network spanning 16 counties and serving millions of customers across diverse demographic
      and economic segments. Throughout this journey, Quickmart has successfully navigated changing consumer
      preferences, evolving market dynamics and broader economic cycles while remaining focused on delivering value,
      convenience and quality to its customers.                                   
                                                                                  
      The Board believes that the Company's success has been underpinned by a disciplined approach to growth, a
      deep understanding of the Kenyan consumer and a commitment to operational excellence. These foundations,
                                                                                  
      together with our continued investments in our stores, supply chain capabilities, technology platforms and customer
      engagement initiatives, position us to capitalise on the attractive long-term opportunities within Kenya's modern
      retail sector.                                                              
                                                                                  
      As the Company enters its next phase of growth, the Board remains committed to maintaining the highest standards
      of corporate governance. We recognise that sound governance is a critical pillar of long-term value creation and
      a key consideration for investors. Accordingly, we are committed to ensuring that Quickmart continues to operate
      with integrity, accountability and transparency in all aspects of its business. The Board will continue to provide
      effective oversight of management, uphold strong risk management practices and ensure that the interests of all
      shareholders are appropriately safeguarded.                                 
                                                                                  
      Transparency, accountability and investor protection are central to our governance philosophy. As a publicly listed
      company, Quickmart will be expected to meet the disclosure, reporting and governance standards applicable to
      companies listed on the Main Investment Market Segment of the Nairobi Securities Exchange. The Board welcomes
      these obligations and views them as an opportunity to further strengthen stakeholder confidence, enhance

        THE  OFFER   AND  THE  SECURITIES   ON  OFFER                             
                                                                                  
      This summary highlights information in this Information Memorandum but does not contain all the information you
      should consider in making your investment decision. Prospective investors should therefore read this summary
                                                                                  
      together with the more detailed information, including the financial summary elsewhere in this Information
      Memorandum:                                                                 
                                                                                  
       1 Issuer                                                                   
                                                                                  
         Quick Mart PLC, a public company incorporated in the Republic of Kenya with registration number PLC-
         6DPTZPBBA and whose registered address is at Quick Mart Building, Ruaka, Old Limuru Road, P.O. Box 2361-
         00621, Nairobi, Kenya.                                                   
                                                                                  
       2 Selling Shareholder                                                      
                                                                                  
         Sokoni Retail Kenya Limited, a private company incorporated in the Republic of Mauritius under registration
         number 158508 and whose address is c/o Rogers Capital Corporate Services Limited, No. 5 President John
         Kennedy Street, 3rd Floor, Rogers House, Port Louis, Mauritius.          
                                                                                  
       3 Legal Status of the Issuer                                               
                                                                                  
         The Issuer was incorporated in the Republic of Kenya under the Companies Act as a private company on 28 April
         2006 under the name “Kids Supermarkets Limited”, and subsequently, pursuant to a special resolution of the
         shareholders, changed its name to “Quick Mart Limited” on 13 January 2008 (being the date of the Certificate
         of Change of Name as issued by the Companies Registry in Kenya).         
                                                                                  
         Pursuant to a resolution of the sole member of the Issuer passed on 25 August 2026, the Issuer subsequently
         converted into a public company and with effect from 22 September 2026, (being the date of the Certificate
         of Change of Name as issued by the Companies Registry in Kenya), the Issuer changed its name from “Quick
         Mart Limited” to “Quick Mart PLC”.                                       
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
         Upon completion of the Offer and admission of the Issuer’s shares to the Main Investment Market Segment of
         the NSE, the Issuer will become a publicly listed company.               
                                                                                  
       4 Principal Objectives of the Issuer                                       
                                                                                  
         The Issuer’s principal objective is to operate a scalable and efficient grocery retail platform in Kenya, offering
         accessible, convenient and competitively priced everyday consumer goods, including food, fresh produce
         and essential household items. This objective is supported by a nationwide network of modern grocery stores
         across urban, suburban and selected regional locations.                  
                                                                                  
       5 Background of the Offer                                                  
                                                                                  
         The Offer comprises an offer for sale of the Offer Shares by the Selling Shareholder. The Offer Shares form part
         of the entire issued share capital of the Company proposed to be admitted to the MIMS of the NSE.
                                                                                  
         The Company has reached a stage of development where the Board and the Selling Shareholder consider that
         admission to the NSE represents an appropriate next step in its evolution. The listing is intended to broaden the
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      QUICK MART PLC | INITIAL PUBLIC OFFER                                       

=== page 31
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                        29        
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
         Company's shareholder base, enhance its visibility and profile within the Kenyan capital markets and provide
         investors with an opportunity to participate in the continued growth of the Company.
                                                                                  
         The Offer also provides the Selling Shareholder with an opportunity to partially realise its investment in the Issuer,
                                                                                  
         following a period of ownership during which the Issuer materially expanded its store network, strengthened its
         management capabilities, enhanced its operating platform and delivered significant growth in revenue across
         a wider geographic footprint. The Offer is consistent with the Selling Shareholder's investment strategy and is
         intended to facilitate an orderly transition to a broader, publicly held shareholder base. The Selling Shareholder
         is expected to retain up to 50% of the Company's issued share capital following completion of the Offer,
         demonstrating its continued commitment to the Company.                   
                                                                                  
         The Offer is not being undertaken as a result of any change in the Issuer 's strategy, operations or outlook. The
         Issuer intends to continue executing its growth plan, including further expansion of its store network, continued
         investment in technology and omnichannel capabilities, and the enhancement of its customer engagement
         and operational platforms.                                               
                                                                                  
         The Board considers that admission to the NSE will further strengthen the Issuer's corporate profile and
         governance framework while supporting its long-term development as a leading modern grocery retailer in
         Kenya. Following completion of the Offer, the Company expects to continue to benefit from the experience
         and institutional knowledge of the Selling Shareholder, the Board and the management team, while welcoming
         new shareholders who will participate in the Company’s future growth and value creation.
                                                                                  
         The Selling Shareholder has confirmed that its partial divestiture of its shareholding in the Issuer will not result in
         any changes to the Executive Leadership Team of the Issuer, or to the terms of their engagement. Each member
         of the Executive Leadership Team is party to a service agreement with the Issuer that is not conditional on, and
         will not be affected by, the level of the Selling Shareholder’s post-Offer shareholding. Save as disclosed in this
         Information Memorandum, neither the Selling Shareholder nor the Issuer is aware of any other arrangement
         or understanding that would lead to a change in the Executive Leadership Team as a result of, or following, the
         Offer.

       16 Basis for Setting the Price of the Offer Shares                         
                                                                                  
         The Offer Price has been determined by the Issuer and Selling Shareholder, in consultation with the Lead
         Transaction Advisors, using valuation parameters referenced under paragraph 15 above and methodologies
         with reference to the following principal factors:                       
         a. the Issuer's historical and projected financial performance as contained in the Reporting Accountant’s ;
                                                                                  
         b. the Issuer's market position, competitive strengths and growth prospects within Kenya's modern grocery
            retail sector;                                                        
         c. the trading multiples of comparable listed companies in selected international markets extracted from
            Refinitiv;                                                            
         d. the trading multiples and dividend yields of selected Kenyan listed companies extracted from Refinitiv;
                                                                                  
         e. prevailing macroeconomic and capital market conditions in Kenya; and  
         f. feedback from investor engagement conducted prior to the commencement of the Offer.
                                                                                  
         The Issuer and the Selling Shareholder have determined an Offer Price of KES 7.50 per share, implying an equity
         valuation of approximately KES 30.0 billion based on the current issued share capital of 4,000,000,0000 shares
         Shares. The Offer Price represents an implied FY2026 P/E multiple of 12.9x, an implied FY2026 EV/EBITDA multiple
         of 5.7x and an implied FY2026 dividend yield of 6.7%. The implied trading multiples are based on the adjusted
         net income and adjusted EBITDA as contained in the Reporting Accountant's Report.
                                                                                  
         The Issuer and the Selling Shareholder believe that the Offer Price reflects a fair valuation of the Issuer, balancing
         the Issuer's established market position and demonstrated track record with the growth opportunities available
         to it and is intended to provide investors with an attractive basis on which to participate in the Offer. Interested
         investors are advised to consult their stockbroker, investment adviser, banker, financial consultant, legal adviser
                                                                                  
         and other qualified advisers, who specialise in the acquisition of shares and other securities.
                                                                                  
       17 Target Investor Categories and Eligibility

         and (iii) Foreign Investors. For allocation purposes, these principal investor categories will be further segmented
         into following Investor Categories:                                      
                                                                                  
            Kenyan Retail Investors                                               
            A natural person who is a citizen or resident of Kenya and is eligible to subscribe for Offer Shares in
            accordance with the terms of this Information Memorandum and applicable laws and regulations.
                                                                                  
            Kenyan Institutional Investors                                        
            Bodies corporate and institutional investors incorporated, established or licenced in Kenya, including
            collective investment schemes and investment banks licensed by the CMA, retirement benefits schemes
            regulated under the Retirement Benefits Act (Cap. 197 of the Laws of Kenya), insurance companies licensed

            under the Insurance Act (Cap. 487 of the Laws of Kenya), banks and other financial institutions licensed by
            the CBK, and such other institutional investors as may be approved by the CMA.
                                                                                  
            EAC Investors                                                         
                                                                                  
            A natural person who is a citizen or resident of another EAC Partner State (excluding Kenya) and any
            company or other body corporate incorporated or established under the laws of another EAC Partner
            State as defined in this Information Memorandum.

         the final terms and conditions of the Offer.

         all other investors in the Offer.

       19 Minimum Subscription Amount                                             
                                                                                  
         The minimum Application size is 500 Offer Shares and in multiples of 100 Offer Shares thereafter. There is no

       20 Minimum Subscription Condition                                          
                                                                                  
         The Offer is conditional upon valid Applications being received and accepted in respect of not less than 75% of
         the Offer Shares (being 1,500,000,000 Offer Shares) by the Offer Closing Date (the “Minimum Subscription
         Condition”).                                                             
                                                                                  
         Consequences of Non-Satisfaction of the Minimum Subscription Condition   
                                                                                  
         If the Minimum Subscription Condition is not satisfied by the Offer Closing Date (or such later date as may be
         approved by the CMA), the Offer shall not proceed and shall be deemed to have lapsed. In such event:
                                                                                  
         a. the Selling Shareholder shall have no obligation to transfer any Offer Shares to any Applicant;
                                                                                  
         b. the Company shall have no obligation in connection with the transfer of any Offer Shares to any Applicant;
                                                                                  
         c. Application Monies received shall be refunded in full to Applicants, within fourteen (14) Business Days of
            the announcement of the lapse of the Offer, by electronic funds transfer to the bank account or mobile
            money account specified in the relevant Application Form; and         
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
         d. neither the Selling Shareholder, the Company nor any of the Advisors shall have any liability to any Applicant
            arising from the non-satisfaction of the Minimum Subscription Condition or the lapse of the Offer, save for
            the obligation to refund Application Monies as set out above.         
                                                                                  
         Waiver or Reduction of the Minimum Subscription Condition                
                                                                                  
         The Selling Shareholder, in consultation with the Company and the Lead Transaction Advisors, reserves the right
         to waive or reduce the Minimum Subscription Condition, subject to obtaining the prior written approval of the
         CMA and compliance with Applicable Laws. Any such waiver or reduction shall be announced in at least two
         newspapers with nationwide circulation in Kenya and on the Issuer’s website prior to the Allotment Date.

         In the event that any Investor Category is undersubscribed, valid Applications within that pool shall be allotted

         following order of priority:

         Applicants may receive fewer Offer Shares than the number applied for. Allocations within an oversubscribed
         pool may be scaled back on a pro rata basis (rounded down to the nearest whole number) or on such other
                                                                                  
         equitable basis as the Issuer, the Selling Shareholder and the Lead Transaction Advisors may determine, subject
         to the approval of the CMA.                                              
                                                                                  
         Multiple CDS Accounts registered in the name of the same applicant will be aggregated and treated as a single
         application for allotment purposes.                                      
                                                                                  
         Amendment of the Allocation Policy

         a fair and equitable allocation of Offer Shares, the Issuer and the Selling Shareholder may amend the allocation
         policy with the prior approval of the CMA. Any such amendment will be announced in at least two newspapers
         with nationwide circulation and on the Issuer’s website or in such other manner as may be prescribed by the
         CMA and the NSE.

            Community Partner State; and

            Act (or the equivalent statute of an EAC Partner State) in which citizens of an EAC Partner State or the

        MACROECONOMIC         OVERVIEW                                            
                                                                                  
       1 Introduction                                                             
      The Issuer’s business is influenced by the macroeconomic conditions prevailing in its principal markets, including levels
                                                                                  
      of economic growth, inflation, exchange rate movements, interest rates, employment and household disposable
      income. During the period under review, these factors affected consumer demand, pricing dynamics, input costs,
      logistics and utility expenses and, more generally, the operating environment for the grocery retail sector. In particular,
      inflationary pressures, changes in consumer purchasing power and movements in currencies and energy costs
      formed an important part of the backdrop against which the Issuer operated. The discussion below summarises
      the principal macroeconomic trends in the Issuer’s key markets during the Historical Period.
                                                                                  
       2 Population and employment                                                
                                                                                  
      Kenya has a large, growing and youthful population, estimated by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (“KNBS”)
      at approximately 54.2 million as at mid-2026 compared with 47.6 million recorded in the 2019 Kenya Population and
      Housing Census. The 2019 census also recorded approximately 12.1 million households, with an average household
      size of 3.9 persons. The population is also increasingly urban, with approximately 18.5 million people (32% of the
      population) living in urban areas in 2025. The urban population is projected to grow at 3.4% CAGR, whilst the total
                                      3                                           
      population is projected to grow at 1.8%, up to 2030.                        
      Kenya’s demographic profile is characterised by a relatively young population. KNBS data indicates that the country
      has a median age of 20.3 years, with approximately 72% of the population aged 34 years and below. This youthful
      population profile is expected to support continued household formation and expansion of the labour force over
      the medium to long term.                                                    
                                                                                  
      Employment in Kenya remains concentrated in the informal sector. In 2025, the total recorded employed population
      (excluding those employed in small-scale agriculture) was 21.6 million, with 18.1 million employed in the informal
      sector. Kenya created approximately 822,100 new jobs in 2025, of which approximately 716,800, or about 90%, were
                    4                                                             
      in the informal sector . Overall employment levels grew at a CAGR of 4.2% between 2021 and 2025.
                                                                                  
      Kenya’s population is distributed across 47 counties, with significant differences in population density, urbanisation,
      infrastructure and household purchasing power. The principal urban and higher-density counties provide
      concentrated consumer markets, while smaller cities and emerging peri-urban centres may present longer term
      growth opportunities.                                                       
                                                                                  
       3 GDP Growth and Economic Activity                                         
                                                                                  
      Kenya is the largest economy by nominal GDP in East Africa and a member of the East African Community, a regional
      bloc of eight partner states. With an estimated population of approximately 54.2 million, Kenya represents a large and
                                                                           5      
      important consumer market within the region. Kenya’s nominal GDP was KES 17.6 trillion (USD 135.9 billion) in 2025 .
      Kenya’s economy is broad-based and the KNBS Economic Survey 2026 indicated that in 2025 the largest contributors
      to GDP included agriculture (approximately 23.2%), transportation and storage (11.8%), financial and insurance
      activities (8.3%), real estate (8.2%), wholesale and retail trade (7.8%); manufacturing (7.1%) and construction (6.5%).
      This sector mix highlights the importance of both household consumption and services activity within the Kenyan
      economy, alongside the continued significance of agriculture and infrastructure-related activity.
                                                                                  
      3 Source: World Bank data, https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL 
      4 Source: 2026 Economic Survey, KNBS                                        
      5 Source: 2026 Economic Survey, KNBS, https://www.knbs.or.ke/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2026-Economic-Survey-Popular-version.pdf
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      QUICK MART PLC | INITIAL PUBLIC OFFER

      Kenya has maintained a trajectory of stable economic growth in recent years, underpinned by structural resilience
      and sectoral diversification. Real GDP grew by 7.5% in 2021, reflecting a strong post-pandemic recovery, before
      moderating to 4.9% in 2022. Growth then strengthened to a revised 5.7% in 2023, before easing to 4.7% in 2024
                 6                                                                
      and 4.6% in 2025 .                                                          
                                                              7                   
      The economy recorded stronger momentum in early 2026, with real GDP expanding by 5.3% in the first quarter of
      2026, compared with 4.9% in the first quarter of 2025. The first-quarter 2026 expansion was broad-based, with all
      sectors recording positive growth, including accommodation and food services, construction, financial and insurance
      activities, information and communication, manufacturing, and agriculture.  
                                                                                  
      Looking ahead, Kenya’s economy is expected to expand through 2026 and 2027, with real GDP growth forecast at
                      8                                                           
      5% and 5.4% respectively , although the outlook remains subject to fiscal, climate-related and external risks.
       4 Monetary Policy and inflation                                            
                                                                                  
      Since the beginning of 2025, the Central Bank of Kenya has pursued a broadly accommodative monetary policy
      stance, reducing the Central Bank Rate (“CBR”) from 11.25% in December 2024 to 8.75% by February 2026, before
      pausing in April and June 2026 as inflationary pressures linked to higher energy and transport costs increased due
      to the US-Iran war.                                                         
                                                                                  
      According to data released by the Central Bank of Kenya, inflation has largely remained within the medium-term
      target band of 5 ± 2.5% over the past five years. Average annual consumer price inflation as measured by the
      Consumer Price Index (“CPI”) was 6.1% in 2021, 7.7% in 2022, 7.7% in 2023, 4.5% in 2024 and 4.1% in 2025. This indicates
      that inflation rose materially above the midpoint of the CBK’s target range in 2022 and remained elevated in 2023,
                                                     9                            
      before moderating sharply in 2024 and remaining below the midpoint in 2025.

       5 Household Spending and Income                                            
      Household spending is a central component of Kenya’s economy. Private consumption accounted for approximately
      76.9% and 77.0% of nominal GDP in 2025 and 2024 respectively, underscoring the importance of household
      expenditure as a driver of economic activity. Household and non-profit institutions serving households final
      consumption expenditure was reported at approximately KES 13.5 trillion in 2025, up from approximately KES 12.6
                                             10                                   
      trillion in 2024, indicating continued nominal growth in spending .         
                                                                                  
      Since 2020, Kenya’s GDP per capita has grown steadily in nominal terms, increasing from approximately US$1,927
      in 2020 to approximately US$2,363 in 2025, representing cumulative growth of approximately 22.5% and an implied
                                  11                                              
      CAGR of approximately 4.2% over the period . Kenya’s GDP per capita is significantly higher than that of its East
      African neighbours (approximately 1.8 times Tanzania’s, 2.0 times Uganda, and 2.5 times Ethiopia’s) and this relative
      position supports Kenya’s role as one of East Africa’s more developed consumer markets, with a comparatively larger
      average income base and stronger potential for formal household consumption.
       6 Foreign Exchange and Currency Movements                                  
                                                                                  
      The foreign exchange market remained broadly stable through 2025 and into the first half of 2026. The Kenya shilling
      closed 2025 at approximately KES 129.05 per U.S. dollar as at 31 December 2025 and stood at approximately KES
      129.49 per U.S. dollar as at 30 June 2026, indicating limited movement over the period. This stability was supported
      by adequate foreign exchange reserves, resilient export receipts and continued diaspora remittance inflows.
                                                                                  
      The usable foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 13.2 billion (5.6 months of import cover) as at 30 June 2026,
      improving from USD 9.2 billion (4.7 months) as at 31 December 2025, offering a sufficient buffer against short-term
      external shocks and supporting market confidence. This meets CBK’s statutory requirement to endeavour to maintain
      at least 4 months of import cover, save for a temporary shortfall to 3.9 months in 2023. Previously, these reserves
      stood at USD 7.3 billion (3.9 months) in 2023; USD 8.0 billion (4.5 months) in 2022 and USD 9.5 billion (5.7 months) in
         12                                                                       
      2021 .                                                                      
      Kenya’s improving economic and fiscal management has resulted in improved sovereign credit ratings. For instance,
      S&P Global Ratings’ latest publicly surfaced action indicated a B sovereign rating with a stable outlook in August
         13                                                                       
      2025 , whilst Moody’s rated Kenya at B3 with a stable outlook following its January 2026 upgrade and reaffirmed
                    14                                                            
      this rating in July 2026 .                                                  
      These positive assessments have enabled Kenya to access international capital markets on more favourable terms,
      supporting infrastructure financing and development goals.                  
                                                                                  
       7 Fiscal Performance and Outlook                                           
                                                                                  
      Kenya’s fiscal position remains characterised by ongoing consolidation efforts, elevated debt-servicing costs and
      revenue-mobilisation challenges. Fiscal performance in FY2024/25 was weaker than initially budgeted, with the fiscal
      deficit widening to approximately 5.9% of GDP, above the original target of 4.3% of GDP, largely due to revenue
      shortfalls and rigid expenditure commitments. The National Treasury attributed the revenue underperformance
      partly to the withdrawal of the Finance Bill 2024 and the related public protests, which disrupted economic activity
      and delayed planned revenue-enhancing measures.                             
                                                                                  
      10 Source: World Bank Development Indicators                                
      11 Source: Economist Intelligence Unit                                      
      12 Source: Central Bank of Kenya, Monetary Policy Committee Statements, Monthly Economic Indicators
      13 Source: S&P Global, https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/-/view/sourceId/101641844
      14 Source: Moodys, https://www.moodys.com/researchandratings/region/africa/kenya/042085

      Public debt remains a key constraint. Kenya’s public debt was estimated at approximately 68.8% of GDP by the
      World Bank, while the National Treasury reported public debt of approximately KES 11.81 trillion, equivalent to 67.8%
      of GDP, as at June 2025. Debt-service costs remain elevated, with interest payments absorbing about one-third of
      tax revenue, limiting fiscal space for development and priority social spending.
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      For FY2025/26, the Government of Kenya targets a narrower deficit of approximately 4.8% of GDP, supported by
      projected expenditure of KES 4.29 trillion and revenue, including appropriations-in-aid, of approximately KES 3.32
      trillion. The resulting deficit of approximately KES 923.2 billion is expected to be financed through both domestic
      and external borrowing.                                                     
                                                                                  
      The fiscal outlook is supported by continued economic growth, with the National Treasury projecting real GDP
      growth of approximately 5.3% in 2025 and 2026, and the World Bank projecting average growth of approximately
      4.9% between 2025 and 2027. However, downside risks remain, including weaker-than-expected revenue collection,
      elevated refinancing needs, high domestic borrowing, exchange-rate pressures and potential external or climate-
      related shocks.

        REGULATORY      OVERVIEW    AND   OPERATING    ENVIRONMENT                
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
       1 Introduction                                                             
                                                                                  
      The regulatory environment applicable to the Company’s business spans consumer protection and competition law,
      food safety and standards, employment and labour law, environmental compliance, data protection and county-
      level licensing requirements. The Company will also be subject to capital markets regulation (in connection with the
      Offer and the Company’s ongoing obligations as a listed entity).            
                                                                                  
      The Company has established internal policies and procedures designed to ensure compliance with all material
      applicable regulatory requirements and maintains active engagement with relevant regulatory authorities.
                                                                                  
       2 Capital Markets Regulation                                               
                                                                                  
      The Company’s Offer and admission of its Ordinary Shares to trading on the Main Investment Market Segment of
      the NSE are subject to the regulatory oversight of the CMA and the NSE. The principal legislation governing these
      matters includes the CM Act, the Regulations, the NSE Listing Rules and the CD Act.
                                                                                  
      The CMA is the statutory body responsible for regulating and supervising Kenya’s capital markets. In connection
      with the Offer, the CMA has approved this Information Memorandum and the listing of the Offer Shares on the NSE.
      Following admission of the Offer Shares on the MIMS of the NSE, the Company will be subject to ongoing disclosure
      and compliance obligations under the CM Act, the Regulations and the NSE Listing Rules, including requirements
      relating to periodic financial reporting, disclosure of material information, corporate governance standards and
      conduct of directors and officers.                                          
                                                                                  
      The NSE is the securities exchange on which the Offer Shares will be listed and traded. The NSE operates under
      the regulatory oversight of the CMA and maintains its own rules and requirements applicable to listed companies,
      including the NSE Listing Rules. The Company will be required to comply with the NSE Listing Rules and any other
      applicable rules of the NSE.                                                
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
       3 Competition and Consumer Protection                                      
                                                                                  
      The Company’s operations are subject to the Competition Act, which is administered by the CAK. Kenya explicitly
      prohibits abuse of buyer power under Section 24A of the Competition Act, which is particularly relevant to large
      retailers’ dealings with suppliers. The Competition Act also prohibits anti-competitive agreements, abuse of
      dominance and other restrictive trade practices. As a participant in the Kenyan grocery retail market, the Company
      is required to conduct its business in compliance with these provisions, including in relation to its dealings with
      suppliers, competitors and customers.                                       
                                                                                  
      The RTCP gazetted on 11 June 2021, applies to retailers operating supermarkets, hypermarkets, or self-selection
      stores in Kenya and is designed to encourage self-regulation and harmonise retailer-supplier engagement. The RTCP
      contains provisions relating to recorded supply agreements, regulated payment terms, prohibitions on cost-shifting
      to suppliers, restrictions on charges for store openings, hospitality, listing and shelf space, and dispute resolution
      through the Prompt Payment Committee and Retail Disputes Committee.         
                                                                                  
      The Company’s supplier relationships are materially conducted in accordance with the requirements of the RTCP.
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                         QUICK MART PLC | INITIAL PUBLIC OFFER

=== page 50
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
         48                                                                       
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      The Consumer Protection Act, which gives effect to Article 46 of the Constitution of Kenya, is administered by
      the Kenya Consumers Protection Advisory Committee. The Consumer Protection Act provides protections for
      consumers against unfair trade practices, false advertising, defective products and other consumer-related matters,
      including the right to quality goods and services, right to accurate pre-contractual information, and remedies for
      defective goods. The Company’s retail operations are subject to these consumer protection requirements, including
                                                                                  
      in relation to product quality, pricing transparency, returns policies and customer service.
                                                                                  
      As at the date of this Information Memorandum, the Company is in material compliance with its obligations under
      the Competition Act and the Consumer Protection Act and has implemented policies and procedures designed to
      ensure ongoing compliance with applicable competition and consumer protection requirements.
                                                                                  
       4 Food Safety and Standards                                                
                                                                                  
      The Company’s retail operations, particularly in relation to the sale of food and fresh produce, are subject to food
      safety and standards regulation. The principal regulatory bodies in this area include the KEBS and the Kenya Food
      and Drugs Authority.                                                        
                                                                                  
      KEBS is the statutory body responsible for developing and enforcing standards for goods and services in Kenya,
      including food products. The Standards Act (Cap 496 of the Laws of Kenya) requires that products sold in Kenya
      meet applicable Kenyan standards. Products must bear the KEBS Standardisation Mark (Diamond Mark of Quality)
      where applicable. Imported goods must undergo pre-export verification of conformity (“PVoC”) or destination
      inspection. The Company is required to ensure that products stocked and sold in its stores comply with these
      standards, including requirements relating to product labelling, packaging, quality and safety.
                                                                                  
      Depending on the categories of goods sold, additional product-specific inspections and permits are required
      from the Kenya Dairy Board (for dairy products), the Pharmacy and Poisons Board (for pharmaceutical products),
      the Pest Control Products Board (for pest control products), and the relevant fisheries authorities (for fish and fish
      products). The Company maintains the necessary permits and conducts regular inspections in accordance with
      these requirements.                                                         
                                                                                  
      The Food, Drugs and Chemical Substances Act (Cap 254 of the Laws of Kenya) regulates the sale and distribution
                                                                                  
      of food and drugs in Kenya, including requirements relating to food hygiene, adulteration and fitness for human
      consumption. The Public Health Act (Cap 242 of the Laws of Kenya) also imposes requirements relating to food safety,
      sanitation and hygiene standards for premises where food is prepared, stored or sold. The Company maintains food
      safety and hygiene protocols across its store network to ensure compliance with these requirements.
                                                                                  
      The Weights and Measures Act (Cap 513 of the Laws of Kenya) governs the use of weighing and measuring equipment
      and ensures accuracy and fairness in trade. The Company’s use of weighing scales and other measuring equipment
      for the sale of products by weight or measure is subject to calibration and certification requirements under this
      legislation. Certificates of Verification must be obtained confirming that all weighing and measuring instruments
      used in trade have been verified and stamped.                               
                                                                                  
      As at the date of this Information Memorandum, the Company is in material compliance with applicable food safety
      and standards legislation and maintains quality assurance and food safety management systems across its operations
      to support ongoing compliance.

       5 Employment and Labour Law                                                
                                                                                  
      The Company maintains a substantial workforce across its store network to support its operations. The principal
      pieces of legislation governing employment relationships include the Employment Act, the Employment and Labour
      Relations Court Act, the Labour Relations Act, the Labour Institutions Act, the Occupational Safety and Health Act,
                                                                                  
      and the Work Injury Benefits Act.                                           
                                                                                  
      The Employment Act establishes minimum standards for employment contracts, working hours, leave entitlements,
      termination procedures and employee protections.                            
                                                                                  
      The Occupational Safety and Health Act (“OSHA”) is enforced by the Directorate of Occupational Safety and Health
      Services (“DOSH”). The Company is required to register each workplace with DOSH and obtain an OSHA Certificate
      of Registration of a Workplace, which must be renewed annually. Periodic safety audits must be conducted by a
      registered safety and health advisor, and comprehensive safety and health risk assessments must be completed
      identifying workplace hazards and mitigation measures. The Company maintains occupational health and safety
      programmes across its store network to ensure compliance with these requirements.
                                                                                  
      As at the date of this Information Memorandum, the Company is in material compliance with its obligations under
      applicable employment and labour legislation, including the Employment Act and the Occupational Safety and
      Health Act, and maintains human resources and workplace safety policies designed to ensure ongoing compliance.
                                                                                  
       6 County Government Licensing and Permits                                  
                                                                                  
      Under Kenya’s devolved system of government, county governments have jurisdiction over certain regulatory matters
      relevant to the Company’s retail operations. The Company operates stores across 16 counties in Kenya and is required
      to obtain and maintain various permits and licences from the respective county governments in which it operates.
                                                                                  
      The principal county-level requirements include Single Business Permits, which authorise the conduct of trade
      and business activities within the respective county and which must be renewed annually before 31 January; Food
      Hygiene Licences for premises handling food products; Food Handler Permits and Health Certificates for employees
      involved in food handling; Fire Clearance Certificates and periodic Fire Safety Audit Reports confirming compliance
                                                                                  
      with fire safety standards; Public Health Compliance Certificates confirming adherence to sanitary and hygiene
      standards; Outdoor Advertising Licences for signage and branding; and Building Occupancy Permits. These permits
      are generally renewable on an annual basis and are subject to periodic inspections by county officials.
                                                                                  
      The Company maintains a licensing and permits compliance programme to ensure that all required permits are
      obtained and renewed in a timely manner. The regulatory requirements and fee structures vary across counties,
      reflecting the decentralised nature of county government administration.    
                                                                                  
      The County Licensing (Uniform Procedures) Regulations, 2025 aim to standardise licensing procedures across all 47
      counties, reducing fragmentation and improving the ease of doing business for retailers operating across multiple
      jurisdictions. The Company continues to monitor the implementation of these reforms.
                                                                                  
      As at the date of this Information Memorandum, the Company holds all material permits and licences required from
      the relevant regulatory authorities, national government and county governments (as applicable) in respect of its
      current operations and maintains a compliance programme to monitor the renewal of such permits on a timely basis.

       7 Alcohol Licensing                                                        
                                                                                  
      Stores of the Issuer that sell alcoholic beverages are required to hold an Alcohol or Liquor Licence issued under the
      Alcoholic Drinks Control Act (Cap 121 of the Laws of Kenya). The Issuer holds the necessary alcohol licences for
      those stores in its network that retail alcoholic beverages.                
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
       8 Music Copyright                                                          
                                                                                  
      The playing of music in commercial premises requires licensing from collective management organisations licensed
      by the Kenya Copyright Board (“KECOBO”), including the Performing and Audio-Visual Rights Society of Kenya
      (“PAVRISK”). The Company maintains the necessary music copyright licences across its store network.
                                                                                  
       9 LPG Regulation                                                           
                                                                                  
      Stores that sell LPG cylinders are required to hold a retail Licence for the sale of LPG (the “Sale of LPG Licence”) under
      the Petroleum (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) Regulations, which is overseen by the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory
      Authority (“EPRA”). The Company currently conducts its LPG retail operations under authorisations granted by
      various Oil Marketing Companies. In addition, the Company has submitted an application to EPRA for the Sale of
      LPGs Licence required for its LPG retail operations.                        
                                                                                  
       10 Environmental Regulation                                                
                                                                                  
      The Company’s operations are subject to the Environmental Management and Coordination Act (“EMCA”), which
      is administered by the National Environment Management Authority (“NEMA”). EMCA establishes the framework
      for environmental management in Kenya, including requirements relating to environmental impact assessments,
      pollution control, waste management and sustainable resource use.           
                                                                                  
      The Company is required to manage waste generated by its operations in compliance with applicable environmental
      regulations. This includes obligations relating to the segregation, storage, transportation and disposal of solid waste,
      organic waste and recyclable materials. Premises that discharge effluent require an Effluent Discharge Licence from
      NEMA. The Company is also subject to regulations governing the use of single-use plastics under the Environmental
                                                                                  
      Management and Coordination (Plastic Bags Control and Management) Regulations, 2018, and must obtain a NEMA
      Plastic Bag Usage Clearance Permit. Environmental Impact Assessment audit reports may be required for compliance
      monitoring in respect of certain operations or developments.                
                                                                                  
      As at the date of this Information Memorandum, the Company is in material compliance with its obligations under
      applicable environmental legislation, including the Environmental Management and Coordination Act, and maintains
      environmental management practices designed to support ongoing compliance.  
                                                                                  
       11 Data Protection                                                         
                                                                                  
      The Company collects and processes personal data in connection with its operations, including customer data
      through its Q-Points loyalty programme, employee data and supplier information. The Company’s data processing
      activities are subject to the Data Protection Act, which establishes a comprehensive framework for the protection
      of personal data in Kenya.                                                  
                                                                                  
      The Data Protection Act, administered by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, imposes obligations on
      data controllers and processors, including requirements for lawful processing, data minimisation, data security, data
      subject rights and cross-border data transfers. The Company is required to register as a data controller with the

       12 Taxation                                                                
                                                                                  
      The Company is subject to Kenya’s tax framework, which is administered by the KRA.

      Act, value-added tax (“VAT”) at the standard rate prescribed under the Value Added Tax Act, withholding taxes
      on various payments, pay-as-you-earn (“PAYE”) in respect of employee remuneration, and excise duty on certain
      categories of goods under the Excise Duty Act (Cap 472 of the Laws of Kenya).
                                                                                  
      The Company is registered for VAT and files periodic tax returns and maintains records in compliance with applicable
      tax legislation.

        INDUSTRY    OVERVIEW                                                      
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
       1 Overview of the Kenyan Retail Sector                                     
                                                                                  
      Kenya has one of the more developed and dynamic retail ecosystems in Sub-Saharan Africa outside South Africa.
                                                                                  
      Its relative maturity is reflected in the presence of scaled domestic and international retail chains, meaningful
      modern-trade participation, increasingly diversified store formats, growing e-commerce adoption and relatively
      developed regional logistics and payments infrastructure. The sector is supported by a population of approximately
      54.2 million, an urban consumer base of more than 18 million and long-term growth in incomes and consumption.
      The retail sector forms part of Kenya’s wider services economy and is closely linked to household consumption, food
                                                                           15     
      distribution, employment, logistics and domestic supply chains. In 2025, the wholesale and retail trade industry
      contributed to 7.8% of Kenya’s KES 17.6 trillion GDP and was a significant driver of employment, representing 13.9%
                      16                                                          
      of the national workforce .                                                 
      Kenya’s total household consumption expenditure in 2025 was USD 104.6 billion (Kes 13.5 trillion) and total retail
                                                                 17               
      expenditure, estimated at USD 22.9 billion (Kes 3.0 trillion), accounted for approximately 22% of this . Kenya’s grocery
      retail market remains characterised by a dual-channel structure, with modern formal retail co-existing alongside
      a large informal and traditional retail base. Modern trade channels include supermarkets, hypermarkets, express
      convenience stores and online-enabled retail formats while traditional informal retail channels, include kiosks
      (“dukas”), open-air markets, independent neighbourhood stores and informal traders. Informal trade continues
      to dominate grocery distribution, particularly outside major urban centres, and accounted for approximately 87%
                                                          18                      
      of total estimated grocery retail spend, or USD 19.9 billion (KES 2.6 trillion), in 2025 . Traditional retail channels
      remain important in Kenya because they offer proximity, small-basket purchases, informal credit relationships in
      some communities, flexible packaging and price points, and access to fresh foods through open-air markets and
      neighbourhood outlets. Modern trade accounted for approximately 12% of total retail sales at USD 2.8 billion (KES
             19                                                                   
      0.4 trillion) .                                                             
      Furthermore, Kenya’s modern trade penetration in the grocery retail market specifically is estimated to be 24% which
      is materially below penetration levels observed in more developed markets such as Saudi Arabia (44%), South Africa
                                     20                                           
      (64%), Mexico (64%), Turkey (64%) and Brazil (71%) . This structural gap underpins a long-term opportunity for the
      expansion of organised retailers with scalable operating models in response to increased urbanisation, consumer
      demand for convenience, and the demand for a broader range of products.
