      Competition Risks                                                           
      The Issuer operates in a competitive retail market and may face increased competition. The Issuer competes with
      other modern retail operators, as well as a large informal retail segment comprising traditional kiosks, open-air
      markets and independent retailers. Increased competition from existing operators, new market entrants, or digital
      and e-commerce platforms could result in pricing pressure, loss of market share or reduced profitability.
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: The Issuer has built a national retail platform with a scaled store network, centralised procurement,
        customer loyalty capabilities and an expanding digital offering. The Issuer monitors its competitive positioning
        on a frequent basis to ensure it maintains its competitive advantage, including tracking competitor pricing on
        key products within different categories and running regular customer surveys to assess price perception and
        service levels relative to principal competitors. This monitoring informs the Issuer’s pricing, promotional and
        assortment decisions, and the Issuer has achieved a substantial improvement in customer price perception
        relative to its principal competitors as a result. The Issuer’s established market position, brand recognition
        and customer relationships provide a competitive foundation, while its investment in operational efficiency
                                                                                  
        and customer engagement supports its ability to respond to competitive pressures.
                                                                                  
      Shrinkage, Theft and Fraud Risks                                            
      In the course of its operations, the Issuer may be exposed to shrinkage, theft and fraud. Retail operations are
      inherently subject to inventory shrinkage, including losses from employee and customer theft, administrative errors,
      supplier fraud and spoilage. The Issuer handles significant cash volumes across its store network, which creates
      exposure to theft and fraud. Failure to maintain effective loss prevention measures could result in material inventory
      and cash losses that adversely affect profitability.                        
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: The Issuer has implemented a comprehensive loss prevention framework across its store network to
        protect its inventory and other assets. All stores are equipped with CCTV systems monitored by independent,
        qualified camera room operators. The Issuer also engages independent loss control personnel who perform a
        range of oversight functions, including unannounced store checks, independent verification of merchandise
        receipts, exit searches of staff, and oversight of cashier activity. Customers are checked on entry to stores, and
        security guards are stationed at parking areas, entrances and other critical locations. Designated supervisory
        personnel, including category buyers, branch inventory leads and branch leadership, are accountable for
        store-level asset security. Fire detection and alarm systems are installed across the store network and are
        monitored by reputable third-party service providers. The Issuer also maintains a dedicated Loss Prevention
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      QUICK MART PLC | INITIAL PUBLIC OFFER                                       

=== page 111
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                       109        
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
        team responsible for investigating and recommending remedial action in respect of anomalies relating to
        inventory, staff or customers.                                            
                                                                                  
        This physical and personnel-based framework is complemented by a structured inventory monitoring and
        financial control process. Shrinkage levels are monitored as a key operational metric. The Issuer undertakes
                                                                                  
        regular cyclic inventory counts, informed by the assessed risk profile of individual stock categories, and
        conducts full store-wide inventory counts at least twice a year, supported by a trained internal team responsible
        for the accuracy and efficiency of the count process; the Issuer’s loss control personnel also perform regular
        surprise stock confirmations as part of this process. The Issuer uses automated exception reporting to monitor
        point-of-sale activity, including voids, refunds, negative inventory balances and inventory ageing, and applies
        electronic security tags to products assessed as higher risk, whether due to susceptibility to shrinkage or
        high unit value. The Issuer’s internal audit function, under its Head of Internal Audit, reviews internal control
        gaps that could give rise to shrinkage events and works together with the Loss Prevention team on related
        investigations. Reflecting these controls, the Issuer maintains a store-level provision for expected shrinkage,
        recognised in its financial statements at approximately 0.5% of sales, which is reassessed and adjusted
        following each physical inventory count to reflect the actual stock position identified. The Issuer’s exposure to
        cash-related theft and fraud is further reduced by its transaction mix, with mobile money (M-Pesa) accounting
        for approximately 64.7% of revenue collections, cards for approximately 9.8% and other non-cash forms of
        payment, including credit sales and gift vouchers, for approximately 4.3%, with cash payments comprising
        the remaining approximately 20.1% of revenue collections in the six month period ending 30 June 2026.
                                                                                  
      Growth Strategy Related Risks                                               
      The Issuer may not be able to execute its expansion strategy successfully. The Issuer’s growth strategy includes
      continued store roll-out, operational enhancement and development of digital capabilities. Execution of this strategy
      is subject to risks including the availability of suitable store locations, landlord negotiations, capital requirements,
      regulatory approvals, competition for sites, store fit-out timelines and the successful integration of new stores into
      the Company’s operating platform.                                           
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: The Issuer has a proven track record of successful store roll-out, having grown its network from
        19 stores at the time of the merger in 2019 to 68 stores as at 30 June 2026, with a target of 73 stores by FY
        2026. Each new store is expected to break even at the EBITDA level from its first month of operation, achieve
                                                                                  
        sales maturity within 12 months on average, and recover its capital investment within two to three years. The
        majority of stores opened to date have met these milestones. The Issuer has not closed any store due to
        underperformance. The only store closure to date was the Shirikisho store, which ceased operations at the
        end of its lease after the landlord elected to repurpose the premises. Despite the costs associated with new
        store openings, the Issuer has remained profitable throughout the review period and has delivered year-on-
        year profitability growth. The Issuer’s flexible store format strategy and disciplined site selection processes
        support continued expansion. The Issuer is also actively developing its digital capabilities to enhance customer
        engagement and expand its reach. Recent initiatives include the launch of a loyalty programme to drive
        customer retention, the QSOKO App to enable online shopping, and integration with third-party delivery
        platforms such as Uber Eats and Glovo to extend convenience and accessibility. Historically, the Issuer’s store
        roll-out has been funded largely through internally generated cash flows.

       4 Industry Risks                                                           
                                                                                  
      Consumer Preferences and Shopping Behaviours Related Risks                  
      Consumer preferences and shopping behaviours may change. The retail industry is subject to evolving consumer
      preferences, including in relation to product choices, shopping formats, convenience and value. Failure by the Issuer
      to anticipate, identify or respond effectively to changes in consumer preferences could result in reduced customer
      traffic, loss of market share and diminished financial performance.         
                                                                                  
        Mitigant:The Issuer operates a comprehensive consumer insight and engagement framework to anticipate
        and respond to evolving preferences. This includes:                       
                                                                                  
         a. monitoring shopping behaviour data across its store network and digital platforms, including through
          its Q-Points loyalty programme, which supports customer segmentation and targeted promotional
          campaigns;

         b. continuous adaptation of product assortment, with particular emphasis on fresh produce quality and
          availability, which the Issuer’s customer data indicates is a primary driver of store visits;
         c. investment in omnichannel capabilities, including the QSOKO digital ordering and delivery platform, to
          serve customers who increasingly expect both online and in-store shopping options;

        The Issuer employs TRFs, its category management software, to support data-driven decisions on assortment,

        convenience-led and localised retail shopping. However, there can be no assurance that these measures

      E-Commerce Related Risks                                                    
      The growth of e-commerce and digital retail may intensify competitive dynamics. E-commerce and digital grocery
      platforms, including quick-commerce services offering rapid delivery, represent an evolving channel in Kenyan
      retail. Increased consumer adoption of digital channels could affect customer traffic at physical stores and intensify
      competitive pressure from both established and emerging digital-first competitors.
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: E-commerce and digital grocery adoption continue to grow in Kenya, and the Issuer has developed
        a range of digital sales channels to complement its physical store network and respond to changing customer
        shopping preferences. In FY2025, the Issuer’s e-commerce sales grew by approximately 90% year-on-year
        to approximately KES 1.1 billion, equivalent to approximately 2.2% of total sales, with sales through the Issuer’s
        QSOKO platform growing at an average monthly rate of approximately 38% during the year. Customers can
        place orders through the QSOKO App, WhatsApp and third-party delivery platforms such as Uber Eats and
        Glovo, in addition to shopping in-store.                                  
                                                                                  
        The Issuer’s e-commerce model is store-led: existing stores serve as the primary picking and fulfilment
                                                                                  
        points for online orders within their respective catchment areas. This approach allows the Issuer to use
        its existing inventory, store infrastructure and geographic footprint to support the growth of online sales
        without requiring separate warehousing or fulfilment infrastructure. The Issuer continues to develop its digital
        channels, delivery capabilities and customer reach as part of its broader strategy to serve customers across
        both physical and digital channels.                                       
                                                                                  
      External Shocks Related Risks                                               
      The grocery retail sector may be affected by external shocks. The retail industry is susceptible to external shocks
      such as disease outbreaks, pandemics, natural disasters, civil unrest or other events that may disrupt supply chains,
      restrict customer mobility or alter consumer behaviour. Such events could have a material adverse effect on the
      Issuer’s operations, revenues and profitability.                            
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: The Issuer’s business proved resilient during the COVID-19 pandemic, during which its stores
        remained operational as providers of essential goods. During the pandemic period, the Issuer achieved like-
        for-like sales growth of 12% and overall basket growth of 32%. For the financial year ended 31 December 2021,
        the Issuer recorded revenue of approximately KES 25.7 billion, representing year-on-year growth of 49.5%
        and operating profit of approximately KES 1.1 billion. This resilience reflects the nature of the Issuer’s product
        offering: food and fresh categories, which comprise predominantly staple and non-discretionary products,

        through periods of external shock. The Issuer also maintains business continuity plans and has developed
        operational flexibility to respond to disruptions, supported by comprehensive insurance coverage, including

      Climate and Environmental Risks                                             
      Climate change and environmental factors may affect the Issuer’s operations. Kenya is exposed to climate variability,
      including droughts, floods and other weather-related events, which could affect agricultural production, disrupt
      supply chains for fresh produce and food products, increase energy costs and damage store infrastructure.
      Changes in weather patterns may also affect consumer behaviour and demand. Environmental regulations, including
      requirements relating to waste management, single-use plastics and energy efficiency, may increase compliance
      costs or require changes to the Company’s operations.                       
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: The Issuer sources products from diversified suppliers, including fresh produce across distinct
        climatic and geographic zones, which reduces its reliance on any single production area and its exposure to
        localised weather-related disruptions. The Issuer also maintains inventory management practices designed
        to respond to supply variability, and monitors environmental regulatory developments to maintain compliance
        with applicable environmental laws and regulations. In addition, the Issuer is taking steps to reduce its
        exposure to energy-cost increases and grid-supply volatility through renewable-energy and energy-efficiency
        initiatives. Its solar photovoltaic system at the Nyali branch, commissioned in February 2026, supplied
        approximately 43% to 44% of that branch’s electricity requirements between March and June 2026, and the
        Issuer has identified 52 further branches as viable sites for rollout over the following 12 months. The Issuer
        is also transitioning to energy-efficient refrigeration and HVAC systems, including retrofit chiller doors, to
        reduce electricity consumption and mitigate exposure to increases in energy costs. Further information
        on the Issuer’s environmental and social management framework and initiatives is set out in paragraph 12
        (Environmental and Social Considerations) of the section entitled “Business Overview and Operations” in
        this Information Memorandum.                                              
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
       5 Risks Relating to the Offer and Offer Shares                             
                                                                                  
      The Offer is Subject to a Minimum Subscription Condition                    
      The Offer is conditional upon valid Applications being received and accepted in respect of not less than 75% of the
      Offer Shares (being 1,500,000,000 Offer Shares) by the Offer Closing Date. If the Minimum Subscription Condition
      is not satisfied, the Offer will not proceed and will be deemed to have lapsed. In such event, the Selling Shareholder
      shall have no obligation to transfer any Offer Shares to any Applicant, the Company shall have no obligation in
      connection with the transfer of Offer Shares, and all Application Monies shall be refunded to Applicants. There can
      be no assurance that the Minimum Subscription Condition will be satisfied.  
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: The Minimum Subscription Condition has been set at a level intended to ensure sufficient demand
        and liquidity in the Offer Shares following listing. The Selling Shareholder, in consultation with the Company
        and the Lead Transaction Advisors, reserves the right to waive or reduce the Minimum Subscription Condition
        subject to the prior written approval of the CMA. Any such waiver or reduction would be publicly announced
        prior to the Allotment Date.

      active trading market will develop or be sustained following admission to listing on the NSE. If an active trading market
      does not develop or is not maintained, investors may have difficulty selling their shares at an attractive price, or at all.

      Interests of the Selling Shareholder                                        
      Following completion of the Offer, the interests of the Selling Shareholder, who will retain a significant shareholding

      The Selling Shareholder may have different investment horizons and return expectations than new investors and
      may take actions, or support strategies, that new investors do not agree with or that benefit the Selling Shareholder
      at the expense of the new investors.                                        
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: Subject to the possible upstream ownership reorganisation of the Selling Shareholder as described
        below and in paragraph 5 (Shareholding Structure (Pre and Post Offer)) in the section entitled "Statutory
        and General Information" in this Information Memorandum, the Selling Shareholder will retain 50% of the
        Issuer’s issued share capital following completion of the Offer. Accordingly, the Selling Shareholder would
        retain a significant continuing economic interest in the Issuer, demonstrating its continued commitment to
        the Issuer’s long-term success. The Selling Shareholder is also subject to lock-up undertakings as set out in
        the section entitled “Lock-up Arrangement” in the section entitled "Statutory and General Information" in
        this Information Memorandum."                                             
                                                                                  
      Certain Shareholders May Retain Significant Influence Over the Issuer.      
      Following the Offer, the Selling Shareholder will hold significant shareholding in the Issuer and may therefore be
                                                                                  
      able to exercise significant influence over matters requiring shareholder approval, such as the election of directors,
      amendments to the Issuer’s constitutional documents and other significant corporate actions. The interests of these
      shareholders on such matters may not always align with the interests of other shareholders.
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: The Issuer has put in place a corporate governance framework intended to provide appropriate
        oversight of matters involving significant shareholders. This framework operates through the Issuer’s Board
        structure, its articles of association, and governance policies addressing matters such as related-party
        transactions and other material corporate decisions. The Board will include independent non-executive
        directors, who provide independent oversight on matters that could otherwise be influenced by significant
        shareholders, in the interests of the Issuer and its shareholders generally. The Issuer has also engaged Adili to
        support the development and implementation of governance structures, policies and procedures appropriate
        for a publicly listed company, including as the Issuer continues to strengthen its governance framework
        following the Offer.                                                      
                                                                                  
      The indirect upstream ownership of the Selling Shareholder may change following completion of the Offer.
      Adenia Capital (IV) LP and Adenia Capital (IV) Parallel LP (together, the “Adenia Funds”), each managed by Adenia,
      together hold an effective economic interest of approximately 48.6% in the Company, indirectly through Sokoni Retail
      Holdings Limited. As part of the ordinary course management of its fund structure, Adenia Partners may, following

      completion of the Offer, undertake an internal reorganisation of the Adenia Funds’ shareholding interests, which may
      involve the transfer of all or part of those interests to an existing fund or to a new fund established and managed by
      Adenia Partners. Any such reorganisation could result in a change in the identity of the fund vehicles that indirectly
      hold that interest in the Company. This risk relates to Adenia’s fund structure only and does not affect the Selling
      Shareholder or its respective interests in the Company. For further details, see paragraph 5 (Shareholding Structure
      (Pre and Post Offer)) in the section entitled "Statutory and General Information" in this Information Memorandum.
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: Any such reorganisation would be purely internal in nature and would occur solely within Adenia’s
        fund and holding structure above the Selling Shareholder. It would not involve any sale, disposal or transfer
        of the Issuer’s shares to any third party, nor would it result in any change in the ultimate management,
        control or stewardship of Adenia’s investment. Any successor vehicle would remain managed, advised and/
        or controlled by Adenia or one of its affiliates, ensuring full continuity in the oversight and management of
        the investment. Importantly, such reorganisation would have no impact on the Selling Shareholder’s direct
        shareholding in the Issuer, the Issuer’s governance, management or day-to-day operations, or the rights and
        interests attaching to the Ordinary Shares held by public shareholders. The purpose of any such reorganisation
        would be limited to internal fund structuring considerations and would not alter the underlying investment
        or the relationship between the Issuer and its shareholders. Any such reorganisation would, in all cases, be
        implemented in accordance with applicable laws, regulations and disclosure requirements, including any
        necessary approvals, or notifications.                                    
                                                                                  
      Future Sales or Issuances of Shares                                         
      Future sales or issuances of shares may adversely affect the trading price. Sales or issuances of substantial numbers
      of shares following the Offer, or the perception that such sales could occur, could adversely affect the trading price
      of the Offer Shares. This includes sales of the Lock-Up Shares by the Selling Shareholder following the expiry of any
      Lock-Up period, or at any time, sales of Shares not subject of the Lock-Up Period, as well as any future capital raises
      or equity issuances by the Issuer.                                          
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: Subject to the risk factor described above under “The indirect upstream ownership of the Selling
        Shareholder may change following completion of the Offer”, the contemplated upstream reorganisation
        would not result in a change of ultimate beneficial ownership of the Selling Shareholder’s interest in the
        Issuer. In accordance with the Regulations and the exemptions granted by the CMA, the Selling Shareholder
                                                                                  
        is subject to lock-up restrictions on the sale of the Lock-Up Shares for a period of twenty-four (24) months
        following the Listing Date.                                               
                                                                                  
      Dividend Payment Related Risks                                              
      Dividend payments are not guaranteed. The Issuer’s ability to pay dividends depends on its earnings, financial
      condition, capital requirements, expansion plans, applicable legal and regulatory restrictions and the discretion of
      the Board of Directors. The Issuer’s dividend policy is set out in the section entitled “Dividend Information” in this
      Information Memorandum. There is no assurance that the Issuer will pay dividends in any particular amount, or at
      all, in any given financial year.                                           
                                                                                  
        Mitigant: The Board of Directors has adopted a dividend policy to guide distributions to shareholders,
        and the Issuer has a consistent track record of dividend payments, having declared and paid dividends in
        each financial year from FY2022 to FY2025. The Issuer has a track record of generating positive cash flows
        and, subject to future performance and capital requirements, intends to balance shareholder returns with
        investment in growth.

      Quickmart’s revenue increased from KES 25.7 billion in FY2021 to KES 50.4 billion in FY2025, representing a CAGR
      of 18.4%, and amounted to KES 27.3 billion for the six months ended 30 June 2026. Revenue growth was driven by
      store expansion and increased same store sales                              
                                                                                  
      Gross profit grew from KES 5.4 billion in FY2021 to KES 11.1 billion in FY2025, with gross profit margin remaining
      broadly stable and improving to 22.5% in the six months ended 30 June 2026. 
                                                                                  
      Operating expenses increased over the Historical Period, from KES 4.5 billion to KES 7.9 billion principally reflecting
      higher employee benefits, administration and general expenses, and higher depreciation and amortisation expenses
      in relation to store leases, consistent with the expansion of the Company’s operations and asset base. Tight cost
      containment supported consistent growth in operating profits.               
                                                                                  
      The Company’s profitability increased significantly over the Historical Period, with EBITDA increasing from KES 2.2
      billion in FY2021 to KES 5.1 billion in FY2025 and EBITDA margins improving from 8.6% to 10.1% over the same period,
      with EBITDA of KES 2.8 billion and an EBITDA margin of 10.3% for the six months ended 30 June 2026. Profit for the
                                                                                  
      year increased from KES 182.6 million in FY2021 to KES 1.5 billion in FY2025, while profit for the six months ended 30
      June 2026 amounted to KES 872.8 million.                                    
                                                                                  
      Overall, the Company’s performance reflects sustained revenue growth, stable gross margins and improving
      operating leverage, resulting in stronger profitability across the periods presented.

      Quickmart’s total assets increased from KES 13.1 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 19.7 billion as at 31 December
      2025. Increases in property and equipment, plus right of use assets recognised under IFRS 16 reflecting the
      Company’s store leases, drove the overall increase in non-current assets, as the Company significantly expanded
      its store network across the country over the period with the addition of 19 stores. This trend continued into the
                                                                                  
      current year, with the addition of 4 stores by 30 June 2026.                
                                                                                  
      Non-current assets represented the largest component of total assets across the periods presented, increasing
      from KES 9.1 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 11.3 billion as at 31 December 2025 and KES 12.3 billion as at 30
      June 2026. Current assets also increased over the Historical Period, from KES 4.0 billion as at 31 December 2021 to
      KES 8.4 billion as at 31 December 2025, driven by inventories and trade receivables as Quickmart’s working capital
      needs increased in line with revenue expansion. The marginal decline in current assets to KES 7.2 billion reported
      as of June 2026 can be attributed to the seasonality of the business, as the festive period in December typically
      generates higher sales which requires higher working capital balances.      
                                                                                  
      The Company’s liabilities increased from KES 11.7 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 18.7 billion as at 31 December
      2025, before decreasing to KES 17.5 billion as at 30 June 2026. Non-current liabilities were comprised principally
      of non-current lease liabilities, which remained broadly stable and continued to represent the largest component
      of non-current liabilities throughout the period. Non-current borrowings declined from a peak of KES 05. billion in
      FY2022 and were fully repaid by June 2026, resulting in a nil non-current borrowing balance as at 30 June 2026.
                                                                                  
      The increase in liabilities in 2025 was driven mainly by higher current liabilities, particularly trade and other payables,
      reflecting the scale of the Company’s purchasing activities and working capital requirements as the store network
      expanded. Current lease liabilities also remained a significant component of current liabilities.

       5 Selected Operating and Other Key Performance Indicators                  
                                                                                  
      The Issuer uses certain alternative performance measures (“APMs”), including EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, Underlying
      Adjusted Free Cash Flow and Cash Conversion Ratio (amongst others), to supplement the measures of performance,
      liquidity and financial position presented in accordance with IFRS. Management believes these APMs provide useful
      information to investors because they facilitate period-on-period comparisons of underlying business performance
      and are used internally to assess and operating results, capital allocation and liquidity.
                                                                                  
      These APMs have limitations as analytical tools and should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for
      the most directly comparable measures prepared in accordance with IFRS. This data has not been audited by the
      Company’s independent auditors. In addition, these measures may not be comparable to similarly titled measures
      used by other companies or market experts. Reconciliations of these measures to the most directly comparable
      IFRS measures are set out in the table below.

      indicated.

      Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA margin                                  
      The Company defines Adjusted EBITDA as operating income plus depreciation and amortisation, less any exceptional
      expenses including management fees, consultancy fees, mergers costs, impacts of political protests, and COVID
      related expenses. Exceptional items are additional specific items that because of their nature or non-recurring
      incidence, are considered to hinder comparison of the Company’s performance on a year-to-year basis. The
      Company’s Directors view Adjusted EBITDA as a useful measure because it is used to analyse the trading performance
      of the business.

      Net Working Capital                                                         
      Quickmart’s receivables primarily consist of supplier rebates and volume discounts. Therefore, the Company’s
      management nets these off against trade payables to calculate net supplier days. The cash conversion cycle is
      then computed as inventory days less net supplier days. Net working capital balances measured at year end reflect
      seasonality as this is the peak trading and restocking month. The following table provides the Net Working Capital
      for the Historical Period.

        OPERATING     AND  FINANCIAL    REVIEW                                    
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      The following discussion should be read together with the sections entitled “Industry Overview”, “Business
      Overview and Operations”, “Selected Historical Financial Information”, and the “Reporting Accountant's
                                                                                  
      Report” including the notes thereto, included elsewhere in this Information Memorandum. This section is intended
      to assist investors in understanding the principal factors that have affected, and are expected to continue to affect,
      the Company’s results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.    
                                                                                  
      The following discussion of the Company’s results of operations and financial condition contains forward looking
      statements. The Company’s actual results could differ materially from those that it discusses in these forward-
      looking statements. Factors that could cause or contribute to such differences include those discussed below and
      elsewhere in this Information Memorandum, particularly under the section entitled “Risk Factors and Mitigants” in
      this Information Memorandum. In addition, certain industry issues also affect the Company’s results of operations
      and are described in the section entitled “Industry Overview” in this Information Memorandum.
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
       1 Overview                                                                 
                                                                                  
      Quickmart's performance over the Historical Period was driven by disciplined store expansion, improving same-store
      productivity and growth in loyalty-led customer engagement. Revenue increased from KES 25.7 billion in FY 2021
      to KES 50.4 billion in FY 2025, supported by store additions, higher basket values and increased customer traffic,
      while operating margins improved as the business scaled and operating costs were absorbed over a larger revenue
      base. The Company maintained positive operating cash flows throughout the period, supported by profitability and
      a structurally negative working capital cycle, while continuing to invest in its store base and meet lease, debt and
      dividend obligations. Looking ahead, management expects further growth to be supported by continued network
      expansion, like-for-like sales growth, private label development and omnichannel initiatives, subject to consumer
      demand, inflation, supplier terms and execution of the store rollout plan.

      A further discussion on the Company’s key revenue drivers follows below.    
                                                                                  
      Revenue Growth Drivers                                                      
                                                                                  
      Store Network Expansion                                                     
                                                                                  
      A significant portion of the Company’s revenue growth over the period was attributable to the expansion of its store
      network. The Company increased its store footprint from 45 stores in FY2021 to 64 stores by the close of FY2025,
      broadening its customer reach and presence to 16 counties.                  
                                                                                  
      In FY2022, Quickmart recorded the highest revenue growth over the period, with sales increasing by 35.4% year-on-
      year. This performance was largely supported by the addition of ten new stores, which accounted for approximately
      half of the KES 9.1 billion increase in revenue during the year. Quickmart continued its expansion strategy between
      FY2023 and FY2025, albeit at a slightly slower pace, opening a further nine stores. During this period, the Company
      prioritised consolidating its performance across its existing store network with a number of initiatives, including
      introducing 24-hour stores and enhancing promotional activities, while continuing to add stores. This combination
      of new stores openings and LFL sales growth supported annual revenue growth rates of 18.5%, 13.3% and 8.0% for
      FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 respectively.                                     
                                                                                  
      As at FY2025, the stores opened between FY2021 and FY2025 generated approximately KES 22.8 billion in revenue,
      equivalent to 45% of total sales. New stores achieve sales maturity within 12 months on average and thereafter
      track like-for-like growth. As illustrated in the table below, average revenue per store and per net selling area (sq.
      ft) showed consistent growth over the period. Average revenue per store grew by 1.2% in FY2025, reflecting the
      inclusion of four stores opened during the year, three of which opened in the second half of FY2025. Adjusting for
      opening dates, average revenue per store grew by approximately 5%.

      Like-for-Like Revenues, Basket Size and Transaction Volumes                 
      Like-for-like revenue growth was supported by increased customer traffic, higher average basket values and pricing
      adjustments across selected product categories. Quickmart has successfully achieved consistent increases in like-
      for-like sales owing to:

         FY2025, with these customers contributing to 74% of total sales in FY2025
                                                                                  
         Growth in the average basket size, supported by targeted pricing strategies and optimised product mix, resulting
         in the average basket size growing from KES 769 in FY2021 to Kes 893 in FY2025
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
         The 24-hour store roll out, extending hours at high-traffic locations attracts a broader customer base and meets
         growing demand for flexible shopping. Night-shift sales represented 15% of participating stores’ sales in FY2025.
         The contribution of after hour sales to total sales was approximately 8% in FY2025
                                                                                  
         Localized product assortment with tailored offerings to meet regional preferences and customer needs

         increases in basket size.

      Sales Contribution by Product Category Mix                                  
      Quickmart’s product mix is anchored in recurring household consumption, and overall, each product category’s
      contribution to total revenue was fairly stable over the period, with the largest contributors to sales being food
      (c.52%), fresh (c.13%), homecare (c.9%) and personal care (c.8%) on average over the Historical Period.
                                                                                  
      Sales Contribution by Geographic Revenue Analysis

      The Company’s revenue base remained concentrated in Nairobi County, reflecting its established and growing
      store footprint in urban neighbourhoods, while newer regions contributed incremental growth as stores opened
      during the period matured. Expansion has strengthened Quickmart’s national footprint and increased access to
      underserved catchment areas.

      E-commerce                                                                  
      The contribution of E-commerce sales, across QSOKO and various third-party platforms increased to KES 1.1 billion
      in FY2025 (2.2% of total sales) from KES 0.6 billion in FY2024, reflecting a year over year growth of 90%. In FY2025,
      sales from QSOKO grew by an average of 38% per month. E-commerce is a nascent but strategic channel, as it
      extends Quickmart’s reach beyond immediate store catchments, enhances convenience, is margin accretive and
      leverages existing infrastructure in a capital efficient manner by reducing upfront expansion capital expenditure.

      Profitability Performance                                                   
      Quickmart’s gross profit, Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted net profit increased significantly over the Historical Period,
      reflecting the combined effect of sustained revenue growth, stable gross margins and improved operating leverage
      as the business scaled. Gross profit increased from KES 5.4 billion in FY2021 to KES 11.1 billion in FY2025, representing
      a CAGR of 19.6%.                                                            
                                                                                  
                 30                                                               
      Adjusted EBITDA , increased from KES 2.6 billion in FY2021 to KES 5.4 billion in FY2025, at a CAGR of 19.9%, with the
      Adjusted EBITDA margin improving from 10.1% to 10.6%, reflecting the Company’s operating leverage as revenue
      and gross profit expanded. The Adjusted net profit margin increased significantly over the same period, from KES
      0.4 billion (adjusted net margin of 1.7%) to KES 1.7 billion (adjusted net profit margin of 3.4%), at a CAGR of 39.7%.

      Gross margins were resilient over the period, increasing from 21.1% in FY2021 to 22.0% in FY2025, supported by
      scale benefits, pricing discipline and successful implementation of the supplier joint business plans, which provide
      for volume-based rebates upon the achievement of sales targets. Gross margin improved most notably in FY2024,
      increasing to 22.0% from 21.0% in FY2023, before remaining broadly stable at 22.0% in FY2025.
                                                                                  
      Operating expenses increased in absolute terms over the period, at a CAGR of 15.4%, driven by higher employee
      benefits, administration and general expenses, as well as depreciation and amortisation costs in relation to store
      leases. The Company exercised effective cost controls, and operating expenses declined as a proportion of revenue
      from approximately 17.5% in FY2021 to 15.8% in FY2025.                      
                                                                                  
      Employee benefits, the largest constituent of operating expenses, increased from KES 1.7 billion in FY2021 to KES
      3.2 billion in FY2025, broadly reflecting the growth of the business and the additional staff costs required to support
      a larger store network and operating platform. As a percentage of revenue, employee benefits improved slightly
      from approximately 6.6% in FY2021 to 6.3% in FY2025, as staff costs were absorbed over a larger revenue base.

      Operating profit before finance cost and tax increased from KES 1.1 billion in FY2021 to KES 3.5 billion in FY2025, at a
      CAGR of 33.2%, while operating profit margin improved from 4.3% to 6.8%. The increase in operating profit before
      finance cost and tax was supported by improved operating cost absorption, partially offset by depreciation and
      amortisation charges relating to property and equipment, right-of-use assets and intangible assets, which increased
      from an aggregate KES 1.1 billion in FY2021 to KES 1.6 billion in FY2025. These charges reflect the asset base required
                                                                                  
      to support the Company’s physical store operations and broader operating infrastructure.
                                                                                  
      Net income increased significantly over the Historical Period, from KES 182.6 million in FY2021 to KES 1.5 billion in
      FY2025, representing a CAGR of approximately 69.5%. Net income margin also improved from 0.7% in FY 2021 to
      3.0% in FY 2025, reflecting the combined effect of revenue growth, improved operating profitability via disciplined
      cost managements and deleveraging.                                          
                                                                                  
      Overall, Quickmart’s profitability profile improved over the Historical Period, as revenue growth translated into
      stronger earnings. The improvement in profitability was achieved notwithstanding higher employee, administrative,
      depreciation and amortisation costs associated with the broader scale of the business.
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
       3 Balance Sheet Analysis                                                   
                                                                                  
      Quickmart’s balance sheet reflects the scale-up of a lease-based grocery retail platform, with growth in store-
      related assets, inventory and trade payables supporting the expansion of the business. Total assets increased from
      KES 13.1 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 19.7 billion as at 31 December 2025, reflecting continued investment
      in the Company’s operating footprint and a larger working capital base.     
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                         QUICK MART PLC | INITIAL PUBLIC OFFER

=== page 134
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
        132                                                                       
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      Asset Base and Investment in Store Infrastructure                           
      Non-current assets increased from KES 9.1 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 11.3 billion as at 31 December 2025,
      primarily driven by property and equipment and right-of-use assets. Property and equipment increased from KES
      4.0 billion to KES 5.3 billion over the same period, reflecting continued investment in the Company’s physical store
      infrastructure and operating platform. Right-of-use assets over the same period also increased from KES 4.7billion to
                                                                                  
      KES 5.2 billion, reflecting the leased nature of the Company’s store network. As at 30 June 2026, non-current assets
      increased further to KES 12.3 billion, supported by increases in both property and equipment and right-of-use assets.
                                                                                  
      Working Capital and Liquidity                                               
      Quickmart’s working capital profile reflects the operating characteristics of a high-volume grocery retail business,
      with inventories (primarily fast-moving) representing the principal current asset and trade payables representing the
      principal current liability. Current assets increased from KES 4.0 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 8.4 billion as at
      31 December 2025, primarily due to higher inventories, trade and other receivables, cash and short-term deposits.
      This reflects the increased scale of the business and the stock levels required to support a larger store network. Trade
      receivables primarily relate to supplier rebates and volume discounts as documented in the supplier Joint Business
      Plans (“JBPs”).                                                             
                                                                                  
      Trade and other payables increased from KES 5.7 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 11.2 billion as at 31 December
      2025, broadly in line with the expansion of purchasing activity and the Company’s increased operating scale. Supplier
      credit therefore remained an important component of the Company’s working capital funding model over the Historical
      Period.                                                                     
                                                                                  
      The Company operated with a structurally favourable, negative net working capital throughout the period, with
      inventory days and net supplier days averaging 41 and 82 days as measured at the year-end dates , translating into
      cash conversion cycle of approximately (41) days. This negative working capital profile is consistent with the dynamics
      of a high-volume grocery retailer, where supplier credit and inventory turnover are important components of liquidity
      management. Net working capital as a percentage of gross sales averaged 9% over the Historical Period.

      Lease Liabilities, Borrowings and Capital Structure                         
      The Company’s liabilities profile remained primarily driven by lease liabilities and trade and other payables. Total
      liabilities increased from KES 11.7 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 18.7 billion as at 31 December 2025.
                                                                                  
      Lease liabilities represented a significant component of the balance sheet throughout the period. Non-current lease
                                                                                  
      liabilities increased from KES 5.1 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 6.5 billion as at 31 December 2025. Current lease
      liabilities also increased from KES 243.7 million as at 31 December 2021 to KES 811.1 million as at 31 December 2025.
                                                                                  
      Significant deleveraging saw bank borrowings decrease from KES 543.1 million as at 31 December 2021 to KES 46.3
      million as at 31 December 2025.                                             
                                                                                  
      Equity, Retained Earnings and Dividends                                     
      Total equity decreased from KES 1.4 billion as at 31 December 2021 to KES 1.1 billion as at 31 December 2025, reflecting
      the net impact of increased profitability and significant dividend payments over the period. Share capital and share
      premium remained unchanged throughout the period, while retained earnings decreased from KES 311.3 million as
      at 31 December 2021 to KES 255.8 million as at 31 December 2025.            
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
       4 Cashflow Analysis                                                        
                                                                                  
      The Company generated positive net cash flows from operating activities throughout the Historical Period, reflecting
      the cash-generative nature of its grocery retail model. Net cash flows from operating activities increased from KES
      2.0 billion in FY 2021 to KES 4.8 billion in FY 2025, at a CAGR of 24.9%, supported by growth in profitability, non-cash
      depreciation and amortisation charges, and working capital inflows, particularly from trade and other payables.
                                                                                  
      Operating cash flow was closely linked to the Company’s negative working capital structure, where inventory
      days are shorter than trade payables days net of trade receivables (primarily consisting of supplier rebates). This
      highlights the importance of supplier credit, inventory discipline and working capital timing to the Company’s cash
      conversion profile.                                                         
                                                                                  
      Net cash used in investing activities remained negative throughout the period, reflecting continued investment in
                                                                                  
      property and equipment, intangible assets and long-term deposits. Purchases of property and equipment were
      the principal investing outflow, amounting to KES 1.2 billion in FY2021, KES 1.8 billion in FY2022, KES 865.5 million in
      FY2023, KES 393.5 million in FY2024 and KES 1.1 billion in FY2025. Over the Historical Period, capital expenditure
      related to maintenance averaged KES 260 million per annum. Quickmart’s investment profile is consistent with the
      capital requirements of a growing grocery retail platform, including store fit-outs, equipment and related operating
      infrastructure. Capital expenditure                                         
                                                                                  
      Despite continued investing activity, operating cash flows were sufficient to cover investing cash outflows in each of
      the historical years presented. Cash flow after investing activities was positive in each year from FY2021 to FY2025,
      increasing from KES 704.5 million in FY2021 to KES 3.7 billion in FY2025. This indicates that the Company’s operating
      cash generation was sufficient to fund capital expenditure and other investing requirements before financing cash
      flows.                                                                      
                                                                                  
      Net cash used in financing activities increased from KES 814.4 million in FY2021 to KES 3.4 billion in FY2025, primarily
      driven by lease liability repayments, dividend payments and repayments of bank borrowings. Lease liability repayments
      increased from KES 827.5 million in FY2021 to KES 1.6 billion in FY2025, reflecting the recurring cash cost associated
      with the Company’s leased store footprint. Dividend payments also increased materially, from nil in FY2021 to KES
      1.6 billion in FY2025, indicating that a meaningful portion of cash generated by the business was distributed to
      shareholders during the period.

       Capital Efficiency and Return on Invested Capital                          
                                                                                  
      Over the Historical Period, the Company's ROIC performance reflected the combined effects of expanding operating
      profitability, disciplined store network growth and efficient working capital management. As new stores matured
      and same-store sales productivity improved, operating earnings increased while the Company's structurally
      negative working capital cycle reduced the amount of incremental capital required to support growth. These factors
      contributed to improved capital efficiency and enhanced returns on invested capital, leading to the growth in ROIC
      from 14.8% in FY2021 to 39.6% in FY2025.

       5 Operating and Financial Outlook                                          
      The Company believes the Kenyan grocery retail sector offers a compelling long-term opportunity, driven by
      favourable demographics, rising urbanisation and the continued shift toward organised retail formats. Leveraging
      its established operating platform, Quickmart expects to continue scaling its store network while preserving margin
      resilience, maintaining an efficient working capital structure and generating strong operating cash flows with prudent
                                                                                  
      capital allocation. Quickmart expects the following growth levels will deliver the next phase of value creation:
                                                                                  
         Maximisation of existing store productivity – higher LFL sales driven by higher average basket sizes, increased
         customer visits and higher sales density, underpinned by Quickmart’s strong value proposition, enhanced
         customer experience through store designs, optimisation of product categories and data driven insights to
         drive promotions.                                                        
                                                                                  
         Disciplined network expansion – leveraging its proven roll-out expertise, Quickmart will continue to open new
         stores in underpenetrated regions, focusing on areas with high residential density and the potential for attractive
         store economics                                                          
                                                                                  
         Scaling its private label (“QuickChoice”) offering – broadening the product range to deepen customer loyalty
         and enhance gross margins                                                
                                                                                  
         Building a scalable, omnichannel ecosystem – extending its reach across physical and digital platforms to enhance
         customer convenience in a capital efficient manner enhancing profitability.
                                                                                  
      These factors are expected to support sustainable revenue growth and attractive returns on invested capital over
      the medium to long term.                                                    
                                                                                  
      H1 2026 Interim Unaudited Financial Results                                 
      In H1 2026, Quickmart recorded strong operational momentum, with an additional 4 stores (opened by 30 June
      2026), an increase in loyalty members from 2.3 million in December 2025 to 2.5 million, and sustained transaction
      growth with an average of 5 million transactions handled per month. As at June 2026, the Company recorded
      revenue of KES 27.3 billion.                                                
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      Profitability margins improved during the interim period with the Company reporting a gross margin of 22.5% (FY
      2025: 22%), an Adjusted EBITDA margin of 10.9% (FY 2025: 10.6%) and an adjusted net income margin of 3.6% (FY
      2025: 3.4%). The Company distributed KES 1.1 billion to its shareholder in the Interim Period.
                                                                                  
      Financial Outlook for FY 2026 and FY 2027                                   
      The Company expects to maintain its current growth trajectory into H2 2026 and FY2027, as it delivers on its strategic
      plan, resulting in projected revenues of KES 58.2 billion and KES 67.4 billion, for FY2026 and FY2027 respectively,
      reflecting a projected growth rate of c. 15% per annum. This growth will be supported by opening of an additional
      5 new stores by the end of FY2026 (increasing the total store network to 73 stores by the end of the year) and a
      planned additional 10 stores (7 supermarkets and 3 hypermarkets) in FY2027. In both years, LFL sales are projected
      to grow at approximately 6% per annum.

      Profitability and Margins                                                   
      The Company expects to maintain EBITDA and net income margins in the range of approximately 10% - 11% and 3% -
      4% respectively for FY2026 and FY2027, broadly in line with recent performance. The Company expects to distribute
      approximately KES 2.0 billion and KES 2.5 billion in dividends in FY2026 and FY2027 respectively, representing dividend
      payout ratios of 95.1% and 90%.                                             
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
      Capital Expenditure                                                         
      Capital expenditure in FY2026 and FY2027 is projected at KES 1.8 billion for each year, comprised of growth capital
      expenditure of approximately KES 1.4 billion and maintenance capital expenditure of approximately KES 0.4 billion.
      The Company will continue to fund its expansion through internally generated cash flows.
                                                                                  
      Working Capital                                                             
      The Company expects to maintain its structurally negative working capital cycle, driven by rapid inventory turnover,
      limited receivables exposure and favourable supplier payment terms.         
                                                                                  
      Cash Flow Generation and Allocation                                         
      The Company expects continued revenue growth, robust margins, disciplined capital allocation, and a negative
      working capital cycle to drive strong cash conversion. This cash generation will fund Quickmart’s organic
      growth strategy, including new store openings, reinvestment in existing locations, and selective digital capability
      enhancements – all financed through internally generated cash flows without reliance on external equity.

      THE SUMMARY BELOW IS INTENDED AS A GENERAL GUIDE ONLY AND DOES NOT CONSTITUTE TAX, LEGAL OR
      FINANCIAL ADVICE.                                                           
                                                                                  
      THIS SECTION PROVIDES A GENERAL OVERVIEW OF CERTAIN TAX CONSIDERATIONS RELEVANT TO THE OFFER
      SHARES, BASED ON KENYAN TAX LAW AND PRACTICE IN EFFECT AS AT THE DATE OF THIS INFORMATION
      MEMORANDUM. THE SUMMARY APPLIES ONLY TO PERSONS WHO ARE THE ABSOLUTE BENEFICIAL OWNERS OF
      THE OFFER SHARES AND HOLD THEM AS INVESTMENTS (AND NOT AS TRADING STOCK OR AS PART OF A BUSINESS
      OF DEALING IN SECURITIES).                                                  
                                                                                  
      THIS SECTION DOES NOT CONSTITUTE A COMPREHENSIVE ANALYSIS OF ALL POTENTIAL TAX IMPLICATIONS
      AND DOES NOT ADDRESS THE TAX POSITION OF SHAREHOLDERS WHO MAY BE SUBJECT TO SPECIAL RULES
      (INCLUDING, WITHOUT LIMITATION, FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS, TAX-EXEMPT ORGANISATIONS, DEALERS IN
      SECURITIES OR PERSONS WHO ACQUIRED THEIR SHARES IN CONNECTION WITH AN EMPLOYMENT RELATIONSHIP).

      STRONGLY ADVISED TO CONSULT THEIR OWN PROFESSIONAL TAX ADVISERS REGARDING THE POSSIBLE TAX
      CONSEQUENCES OF ACQUIRING, HOLDING OR DISPOSING OF THE OFFER SHARES, AS WELL AS RECEIVING
      DIVIDENDS OR OTHER DISTRIBUTIONS, UNDER THE LAWS OF THEIR RESPECTIVE COUNTRIES OF RESIDENCE,
      CITIZENSHIP OR DOMICILE.                                                    
                                                                                  
      Dividend Payments                                                           
      Dividend payments to Kenyan resident shareholders and citizens of East African Community Partner States are
                                                                                  
      subject to withholding tax at a rate of 5%.                                 
                                                                                  
      Non-resident shareholders are subject to withholding tax on dividends at a rate of 15% (or such lower rate as may
      apply under an applicable double taxation treaty). Withholding tax on dividends is a final tax under Kenyan law. Non-
      resident shareholders may be entitled to a foreign tax credit in their home jurisdiction under applicable domestic tax
      laws or double taxation treaties. Shareholders who are exempt from withholding tax under the Income Tax Act or any
      applicable treaty having the force of law in Kenya must provide a certified copy of a valid tax exemption certificate
      or certificate of tax residence to the Issuer (in a form satisfactory to the Issuer) in order to benefit from the relevant
      exemption or reduced rate.                                                  
                                                                                  
      Capital Gains Tax                                                           
      As long as the Offer Shares will remain listed and traded on the NSE, gains realised by shareholders on the transfer
      or disposal of Offer Shares on the NSE are currently exempt from capital gains tax in Kenya.
                                                                                  
      Stamp Duty                                                                  
      As long as the Offer Shares remain listed on the NSE, no stamp duty, registration fees, or similar taxes are payable
      in Kenya on the transfer of such Offer Shares, in accordance with current legislation.
